questions.question: A student looks through a prism at two lamps. The white-hot filament of an old light bulb spreads into a smooth band of every colour from red to violet. The thin glowing gas in a neon sign's tube breaks instead into many sharp bright lines, mostly red and orange. What do those lines show about neon's atoms?
questions.answer: They give off energy only in set amounts
choices: They give off energy only in set amounts
They give off every colour, most too faint to see
They soak up most colours and give back the rest
They give off light only while the gas is burning
questions.context: An electron in a neon atom can sit only at set energy levels, so when the current's electrons knock it up and it drops back, the atom gives off one set amount of energy, a photon of one exact colour; neon's set drops make its set lines, among them a bright red one at 640 nanometres. Between the lines the thin gas gives off no light at all, while the filament, a hot solid, glows in every colour at once. Nothing burns in the tube, and the light is the gas's own, not light it takes in from somewhere else.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade physical science (TEKS IPC 7D, NGSS HS-PS4-3) teaches that atoms give off light of set colours as electrons drop between energy levels, unlike the smooth glow of a hot solid.

questions.question: An electron in a hydrogen atom, lifted to the third energy level, can fall straight back to the first and give off one ultraviolet photon. It can instead fall in two steps: to the second level, giving off a red photon, and then to the first, giving off another ultraviolet one. How do the two photons' energies together compare with the single photon's?
questions.answer: The same, as both ways start and end at the same levels
choices: The same, as both ways start and end at the same levels
More, as two drops give off more energy than one
Less, as a red photon carries less energy than ultraviolet
Less, as some energy is lost in the stop between drops
questions.context: A photon carries exactly the energy its electron loses in the fall, and the fall from the third level to the first is the same however it is made. In electronvolts, a tiny unit of energy, the red photon at 656 nanometres carries about 1.9 and the ultraviolet one at 121.6 carries 10.2, together 12.1, just what the single photon at 102.6 nanometres carries. Walther Ritz found such sums among the frequencies of spectral lines in 1908, five years before Niels Bohr's levels explained them.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders use energy levels to reason about light: a photon carries the energy of its electron's fall, so a fall made in two steps gives off the same total as one.

questions.question: A chemistry class dips clean wires into salts and holds each one in a Bunsen burner's flame. A strontium salt turns the flame crimson, a copper salt green-blue and a sodium salt bright yellow. Through a prism each colour breaks into thin lines, and no two metals' lines fall in the same places. Why does each element give off colours of its own?
questions.answer: Its electrons' energy levels are spaced in its own way
choices: Its electrons' energy levels are spaced in its own way
It burns in the flame at a temperature of its own
It strains its own colours out of the flame's light
Its atoms' weight sets the colours that they give off
questions.context: An electron can only drop between its own atom's levels, and each element's levels are spaced differently, so its drops, and the colours they give, are its alone: sodium's two yellow lines sit at 589.0 and 589.6 nanometres. The flame's heat only lifts the electrons and does not choose the colour, and firework makers rely on the same fact, with strontium for red, copper for blue and sodium for yellow. Lithium also turns a flame crimson, so a careful chemist checks the lines as well as the colour.
questions.grade_note: The emission spectrum as each element's fingerprint, met in the flame-test lab, is a standard ninth-grade chemistry and physical-science topic.

questions.question: Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff began reading the bright lines of metals in a flame through a prism at Heidelberg in 1859. They burned each metal as a chloride, a bromide, an iodide, an oxide, a sulphate and a carbonate, in flames of sulphur, alcohol, lighting gas, hydrogen and more, some far hotter than others. What did they find about each metal's lines?
questions.answer: They kept their places whatever the compound or flame
choices: They kept their places whatever the compound or flame
They moved with the compound but not with the flame
They moved with the flame but not with the compound
They moved with both the compound and the flame
questions.context: In their words, the compounds, the chemistry of the flames and the great differences in their temperatures 'had no influence on the position of the spectral lines corresponding to the individual metals.' Changing everything except the metal is what let a pattern of lines name the element and nothing else, and their test was so sensitive that the eye could catch less than a three-millionth of a milligram of a sodium salt. Their paper of 1860 said the method could be turned on the Sun and the bright stars.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science teaches controlled variables, and Bunsen and Kirchhoff's tests are the experiment behind the claim that spectra identify elements.

questions.question: Joseph von Fraunhofer, a Bavarian lens maker, found hundreds of dark lines in sunlight in 1814. Later he fixed a prism to a telescope and turned it on the night sky. The light of the Moon, Venus and Mars showed the Sun's own dark lines, while the bright stars Sirius and Castor showed lines unlike the Sun's. Where must those lines of Sirius and Castor have been made?
questions.answer: In the stars, before their light set out
choices: In the stars, before their light set out
In Earth's air, as their light came down
In the prism, as their light passed through
In the lens, as their light was gathered
questions.context: The Moon and the planets shine by sunlight they reflect, so they carry the Sun's lines; the stars' light came through the same air, prism and lens, so lines found in Sirius and Castor but not in sunlight had to be made in the stars. Fraunhofer had already got the same lines in sunlight with different glass, which ruled out flaws in it, though two broad bands at the red end of sunlight really are made by oxygen in Earth's air. He never learned what made the lines, and died in 1826.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn that spectra reveal what stars are made of, and reasoning from what changed and what stayed the same is the grade's core evidence skill.

questions.question: Auguste Comte wrote in 1835 that the chemical make-up of the stars could never be studied by any means. A flame coloured with sodium shows two bright yellow lines in exactly the place of the two dark D lines in sunlight. Gustav Kirchhoff sent bright sunlight through such a flame into his spectroscope in 1859, and the dark D lines grew darker. What did that show?
questions.answer: Sodium gas soaks up the very colours it gives off
choices: Sodium gas soaks up the very colours it gives off
The flame's glare makes the lines look darker by contrast
The flame's heat bends the yellow sunlight off its path
Sunlight's yellow waves cancel out the flame's yellow
questions.context: A gas takes up light of exactly the energies its electrons can jump by, the same energies it gives off when they drop back, so a sodium flame with brighter light behind it cuts dark lines where its bright ones would be. The Sun's glowing surface shines out through cooler gas above it, and Kirchhoff concluded that sodium is in the Sun's atmosphere. Comte had died in 1857, two years before the Sun's chemistry was first read from its light.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade physical science teaches absorption spectra alongside emission spectra and how they reveal the elements in the Sun and stars.

questions.question: Pierre Janssen in India in August 1868, and Norman Lockyer in England that October, saw a bright yellow line in the light from the Sun's edge. It lay close to sodium's two yellow lines but on neither, and Lockyer named the element he believed made it helium, after the Greek word for the Sun. The idea met doubt, and even mockery, for 27 years. What finally settled the question?
questions.answer: A gas from a uranium mineral glowed with that line
choices: A gas from a uranium mineral glowed with that line
The line turned up in the light of other stars too
The line was seen again at every eclipse that followed
A gas from a natural gas well glowed with that line
questions.context: William Ramsay treated cleveite, a uranium mineral, with acid in March 1895 and collected a gas whose glow showed the Sun's yellow line, and Lockyer and William Crookes confirmed it as helium; helium was found in natural gas, its main source today, only in 1905, in wells drilled in Kansas. A line seen again at eclipses or in other stars showed only that the line was real, not what made it. The doubters had reason to wait: a green line in the Sun's corona was blamed on a new element, coronium, until it turned out in the 1930s to be iron stripped of 13 electrons by the corona's heat.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn helium's discovery in the Sun as the classic case of spectroscopy, and why a claim waits for confirmation by an independent test.

questions.question: Hydrogen's dark lines are strong in the spectrum of Sirius, weaker in the Sun's and weaker still in Betelgeuse's. Cecilia Payne, at Harvard in 1925, read such lines with Meghnad Saha's new theory of how atoms lose electrons. What did she find mostly sets how strong the lines are?
questions.answer: How hot the star's surface is
choices: How hot the star's surface is
How much hydrogen the star holds
How big the star is
How old the star is
questions.context: Astronomers had long taken a strong line to mean a lot of an element. In the hottest stars nearly all the hydrogen has lost its electron and can make no lines, and in cooler stars such as the Sun nearly all of it sits in its lowest level, where it cannot take up visible light; only near 10,000 kelvins, about the heat of Sirius's surface, are many hydrogen atoms ready to make the lines. Read this way, stars turned out to differ mainly in temperature and to be made mostly of hydrogen and helium, and about 73 percent of the Sun's mass is now known to be hydrogen.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science on stars and spectra teaches that stellar spectra differ mainly by temperature, and Payne's thesis is the classic case.

questions.question: Cecilia Payne's 1925 thesis found far more hydrogen in the stars than anyone expected. Henry Norris Russell of Princeton, a leading astronomer and an examiner of her thesis, wrote to her: "It is clearly impossible that hydrogen should be a million times more abundant than the metals." She added a line calling her figures "almost certainly not real." Why did Russell think it impossible?
questions.answer: He held that the Sun was made much as Earth is
choices: He held that the Sun was made much as Earth is
He held that hydrogen is too light for a star to hold
He held that hydrogen would have burned away long ago
He held that her photographs of the stars were faulty
questions.context: Most astronomers then took the stars to be made of the same elements as Earth in much the same proportions, and Russell strongly supported the idea that Earth and the Sun share one make-up. Four years later he reached her answer by a different method and wrote that the most important earlier measure was 'that by Miss Payne', though for years the discovery was credited chiefly to him. Otto Struve later called hers the most brilliant thesis ever written in astronomy.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn that a reasonable but wrong belief can hold back new evidence, and that a result found again by an independent method is what settles it.

bab30d89f9.why: Fact-check (error): neon gives many lines, not 'a few', and 640 nm is a bright red line, not the strongest. The stem now says 'many sharp bright lines' and the context 'neon's set drops make its set lines, among them a bright red one at 640 nanometres' (F39). Judge (low): 'the same every time' leaned toward set amounts and is cut. 'Every colour, and the tube's glass holds most back' was ruled out by the stem's own bulb, whose glass passes every colour, and some sign tubes really are tinted; it is replaced by 'every colour, most too faint to see', a misconception that does explain lines (wrong: a thin gas gives light only at its own wavelengths, F3).

a7bcb80c7d.why: Judge (high): it re-asked T4's fact that violet carries more energy than red, and 'a far bigger drop' killed both 'less energy' choices. Rewritten on the judge's lines to key what the levels mean for the energy of the light: a fall in two steps gives the same total as one (Ritz's combination principle as Bohr's levels explain it). Hydrogen's Lyman lines and its level energies were sourced first (F34, F35). Each choice carries a reason, one of them true but misapplied (a red photon does carry less than ultraviolet); the stem never says that each element's levels are its own. Fact-check (uncertain, 'about twice'): the old context is gone.

39cfaf2510.why: Judge (medium): the key was the only find on Earth and the only specific choice. 'Its place was measured again, far more exactly' is replaced by a second find on Earth that would also have confirmed helium, but came ten years too late: helium in natural gas, analysed in 1905 (F37). The player must now know which find happened. The stem is unchanged.

00681cd038.why: Judge (medium): 'Astronomers had long read a strong line as a lot of an element' with 'read the lines again' ruled out the amount of hydrogen, the one strong lure; distance and speed were dead; and the colour roster handed over T4's colour as temperature. The old reading moves to the context, the stars are named without their colours (Sirius strong, the Sun weaker, Betelgeuse weaker still, F38), and the lures are now the amount of hydrogen, the star's size and its age, in four short parallel choices so the key is no longer the longest or the only specific one.
